fatal_errors: The proposed sulfur/phosphorus alloying intervention does not reconstruct the CoCrFeNiMox-Ni/MoS2-Ag-Cr2O3 composite or the controlled variation of Mo content.

It treats lubrication as arising from lubricious elements dissolved in a solid solution, missing the distinct roles of Mo-induced lattice distortion, the hard sigma phase, MoS2, Ag, and high-temperature oxide/silver-molybdate tribofilms.

The claimed boundary of -200 to 1000 degrees Celsius and 0 to 1000 MPa is invented and conflicts with the target dry-sliding tests in air from room temperature to 800 degrees Celsius under an 8 N load.

None of the cited evidence supports sulfur- or phosphorus-alloyed HEAs as wide-temperature self-lubricating materials; the sources concern fusion environments, nanoprecipitation strengthening, and general refractory-HEA properties.
The answer provides no specific composition, processing route, quantitative mechanical or tribological result, or temperature-dependent transition in wear mechanism.
explanation: The hypothesis recognizes the broad need for HEA-based materials combining high-temperature mechanical performance with reduced friction and wear, but it does not identify the target material or its operative design. The relevant material is an SPS-fabricated CoCrFeNiMox composite containing Ni-coated MoS2, Ag, and Cr2O3, with Mo1 giving the best overall high-temperature wear performance. Its behavior depends on Mo solid-solution and sigma-phase strengthening plus temperature-dependent lubricant films: MoS2/Ag at lower temperatures and compact NiO/silver-molybdate glaze layers at 600-800 degrees Celsius. The generated proposal instead introduces unsupported sulfur or phosphorus alloying, asserts an unspecified solid-solution mechanism, and supplies fabricated operating limits. Its generic alloyed-versus-unalloyed tribology test is weakly falsifiable, but it would not discriminate the target mechanisms without phase analysis, wear-track chemistry, and temperature-resolved testing. The cited papers do not validate the central intervention or mechanism.
